metadata.title: Capecitabine 825 mg/m² and Radiotherapy – 7 day
metadata.partial_assessment_note: Any independently actionable entered value is assessed; omitted domains remain unassessed and do not block a partial result.
metadata.partial_assessment_policy: Each entered value is assessed independently. Organ-function values or categories are optional; omitted domains remain unassessed and are never assumed normal.

catalogue_reconciliation.scope_note: The NCCP states that its website list is not comprehensive. This reconciliation does not assert that every possible national regimen is published online.

encoding_maturity.label: Source-reconciled organ-function encoding · clinical/pharmacy review pending
encoding_maturity.scope_note: Official binary NCCP PDF retrieved and checked; clinical, pharmacy and patient/PPI review remain pending.

organ_function_reconciliation.note: Structured renal/hepatic component rules were reconciled to the current official NCCP regimen source. Independent Consultant and oncology-pharmacy validation remains pending.

metadata.catalogue_source_check_scope: Catalogue presence and source link structure only; not rule level source fidelity.

provenance.note: 00586 specifies maximum 5–6 weekly cycles; confirm individual radiation course.

metadata.schedule_summary: Take capecitabine twice daily on Days 1–5 of each 7-day cycle with radiotherapy, for a maximum of 5–6 cycles. Days 6–7 are not routine tablet days. Follow the team’s written instructions if radiotherapy or tablets are interrupted.

clinical_governance.prescriptive_authority: The treatment plan must be initiated by a Consultant Medical Oncologist or other appropriately authorised specialist named in the current NCCP source.
clinical_governance.dose_modification_note: Use the most restrictive applicable component rule and confirm dose changes against the current official NCCP PDF.
clinical_governance.disclaimer: Decision-support encoding derived from NCCP 00586 Version 3. It does not replace the current official regimen, prescribing review, pharmacy verification or independent clinical judgement.
clinical_governance.organ_function_rule_status: Source mapped in SACTCheck v0.83.4, with declared source discrepancies; independent Consultant and oncology-pharmacy validation pending.

treatment.schedule_summary: Concurrent radiotherapy and capecitabine Days 1–5 of each 7-day cycle, maximum 5–6 cycles. Radiation decisions require the radiation oncology plan.

diarrhoea_grade.label: Current diarrhoea grade

options.label: Grade 0
options.description: Usual bowel pattern.

options.label: Grade 1
options.description: NCCP low-grade band: 2–3 extra stools/day; source nocturnal-stool wording overlaps grade 2.

options.label: Grade 2
options.description: 4–6 extra stools/day or nocturnal stools (NCCP table 4).

options.label: Grade 3
options.description: 7–9 extra stools/day or incontinence (NCCP table 4).

options.label: Grade 4
options.description: 10 or more extra stools/day or grossly bloody diarrhoea; parenteral support may be needed (NCCP table 4).

diarrhoea_grade.assessment_guidance: NCCP Table 4 uses legacy diarrhoea bands. Nocturnal stools appear in both low-grade and grade-2 rows: clarify the grade clinically. Assess hydration, stoma output, fever, pain and need for urgent care; do not grade by stool count alone.

hand_foot_syndrome_grade.label: Palmar-plantar erythrodysaesthesia (hand-foot syndrome) grade

options.label: Grade 0 — No toxicity
options.description: No palmar–plantar erythrodysesthesia.

options.label: Grade 1 — Mild
options.description: Minimal skin changes or dermatitis, such as erythema, oedema or hyperkeratosis, without pain.

options.label: Grade 2 — Moderate
options.description: Painful skin changes, including peeling, blisters, bleeding, fissures, oedema or hyperkeratosis; limits instrumental activities of daily living.

options.label: Grade 3 — Severe
options.description: Severe painful skin changes; limits self-care activities of daily living.

patient.purpose: Capecitabine tablets help pelvic radiotherapy work against locally advanced rectal cancer. Your team explains how this course fits with surgery and any other chemotherapy.

agents.name: Capecitabine
agents.explanation: After you swallow capecitabine, your body changes it into fluorouracil. This interferes with the DNA and RNA processes cells use to grow. Normal cells can also be affected, which helps explain mouth soreness, bowel symptoms and changes in blood counts.
agents.watch: Stop tablets and contact the team for significant diarrhoea, painful mouth ulcers, hand-foot soreness affecting activities, fever or dehydration. Chest pain needs urgent assessment. Do not restart until instructed.
risks: Severe early toxicity, including DPD-related toxicity

agents.name: Pelvic radiotherapy
visual: Cells lose the ability to multiply
agents.explanation: Radiation is directed at the planned area. Capecitabine helps sensitise cancer cells to it. Nearby bowel, bladder and skin may also become irritated. Effects can build over the weeks and may continue after the final session.
agents.watch: Tell the radiotherapy team about diarrhoea, pain, skin soreness or urinary changes. Discuss possible longer-term bowel, bladder, sexual and fertility effects before treatment.

support.text: No automatic high/moderate IV antiemetic course for capecitabine. Written tablet-day and missed/held-dose instructions; do not double doses or extend to weekends without the team’s plan. Diarrhoea/dehydration, hand-foot and pelvic skin care; nutrition and urgent-contact support.

logistics.title: Tablets, visits and practical planning
logistics.intro: A simple guide to what happens before treatment, on treatment days and at home. Your own service confirms appointments and prescriptions.

steps.title: Before the first dose
steps.text: Confirm DPD results, blood tests, kidney/liver checks and the treatment aim. Keep a current medicine list.

steps.title: Get the tablet plan
steps.text: Check the number of 150 mg and/or 500 mg tablets in each dose and exactly which days to take them. Bring questions to the oncology pharmacist.

steps.title: Plan your visits
steps.text: Attend radiotherapy planning and treatment appointments. Follow the centre’s bladder/bowel preparation instructions; ask how bank holidays or a missed session affect tablets.

steps.title: Take tablets with food
steps.text: Take the prescribed morning and evening doses with or within 30 minutes of food, swallowed whole with water. If swallowing is difficult, contact pharmacy for a safe plan.

steps.title: Know when to pause
steps.text: Significant diarrhoea, painful mouth or hands/feet, fever, sudden illness or dehydration: stop tablets and call. A missed or vomited dose is not replaced.

steps.title: Review and next steps
steps.text: Do not restart after a toxicity break without instructions. Bring your symptom record and remaining tablets if requested. Return unused tablets to pharmacy.

details.title: Keeping tablets safe
details.text: Keep the original labelled packaging away from children. Follow the storage label and pharmacy handling instructions. Do not share tablets or discard them in household waste.

details.title: If treatment is interrupted
details.text: Tell the team which doses were missed and why. Never extend the course, double a dose or move tablet days yourself. Ask for a revised written plan.

details.title: Questions about your appointments
details.text: Ask about transport, blood-test location, pharmacy collection and a named contact for appointment changes. Booking arrangements differ between centres.

details.title: Radiotherapy planning and recovery
details.text: The radiation team plans the field and explains positioning and preparation. Treatment-related bowel, bladder and skin effects can continue after the last session; keep reporting them.

sections.title: Treatment phases and appointments
sections.text: Take capecitabine twice daily on Days 1–5 of each 7-day cycle with radiotherapy, for a maximum of 5–6 cycles. Days 6–7 are not routine tablet days. Follow the team’s written instructions if radiotherapy or tablets are interrupted.

sections.title: Checks after treatment
sections.text: Keep reviewing bowel, bladder, skin, fatigue and nutrition effects during and after the course. Late effects and surgical assessment follow the radiation/colorectal team plan. Do not automatically extend tablets to make up missed radiation days or continue beyond the planned course.

sections.title: Access and practical support
sections.text: No IV port or infusion pump is needed for capecitabine itself; separate treatments may differ. Radiation appointments, tablet supply, meals and transport should be planned together.

chapters.title: Your treatment aim and duration
chapters.intro: The same medicine can be used for different purposes.

items.title: Why this treatment?
items.text: Capecitabine tablets are given with pelvic radiotherapy for locally advanced rectal cancer. The tablets help the radiation treatment work; your team confirms how this fits with surgery and other treatment.

items.title: How long?
items.text: The NCCP weekly schedule runs for up to 5–6 cycles with radiotherapy. The radiation oncologist specifies the dose, field and visits; the MDT confirms later surgery or other therapy.

items.title: Alternatives and decisions
items.text: Discuss the expected benefit, burdens, reasonable alternatives and the option of supportive care. The best choice depends on your cancer, fitness and preferences.

chapters.title: Taking capecitabine safely
chapters.intro: Tablets are active chemotherapy, with a specific schedule.

items.title: Meals and doses
items.text: Use your current prescription. Swallow tablets whole with water with or within 30 minutes after food. Do not cut, chew or crush them; ask pharmacy if swallowing is difficult.

items.title: Missed doses or vomiting
items.text: Do not replace a missed or vomited dose. Never double the next dose. Contact the team for repeated vomiting or uncertainty about the schedule.

items.title: Pause and restart
items.text: Stop tablets for significant diarrhoea, painful mouth/hand-foot symptoms affecting activity, fever or dehydration and seek advice. A toxicity-related pause requires instructions before restart.

items.title: Different tablet strengths
items.text: Different strengths may be combined to make your dose. A reduction changes tablet numbers: use the new label and do not calculate a change from this page.

chapters.title: Your radiotherapy visits
chapters.intro: The radiation team gives a separate, individual plan.

items.title: Before treatment
items.text: Planning appointments define the area to treat and how you will be positioned. Follow the exact bowel and bladder preparation instructions from your centre.

items.title: Daily sessions and tablets
items.text: NCCP 00586 specifies capecitabine Days 1–5 of each week. Confirm the plan if a session is missed, postponed or falls around a bank holiday; do not add weekend tablets yourself.

items.title: After the course
items.text: Side effects can accumulate and continue after treatment. Ask about follow-up and possible late bowel, bladder, sexual or fertility effects.

chapters.title: Tests and checks
chapters.intro: Monitoring helps the team decide whether treatment can continue.

items.title: DPD testing
items.text: DPD helps break down fluoropyrimidine medicines. Low activity can cause severe toxicity; testing before treatment helps guide the plan but cannot prevent every serious reaction.

items.title: Blood, kidney and liver results
items.text: Counts, kidney and liver function are checked before each cycle. Diarrhoea and poor intake can worsen kidney function and make tablets harder to tolerate.

items.title: Your symptoms matter
items.text: Report bowel frequency, stoma output, mouth soreness, hand-foot pain, chest symptoms and what daily activities you can no longer manage.

items.title: Additional checks
items.text: Radiotherapy reviews also address pelvic skin, bowel, urinary and nutritional problems.

chapters.title: Recognise symptoms and act
chapters.intro: Do not wait for the next appointment if you feel unwell.

items.title: Bowel and hydration
items.text: Report diarrhoea or increased stoma output early. Inability to drink, dizziness, very little urine, severe pain or blood in stool needs prompt assessment.

items.title: Hands, feet and mouth
items.text: Pain, cracking, peeling or ulcers that affect normal activities or eating/drinking need advice. Gentle preventive care helps, but does not replace reporting.

items.title: Chest symptoms and infection
items.text: Stop capecitabine and seek urgent assessment for chest pain. Fever, shaking chills or sudden illness needs immediate oncology contact, even if the temperature is normal.

items.title: Treatment-specific effects
items.text: Pelvic radiation can cause bowel, bladder and skin irritation, with possible later effects. Ask about sexual health and fertility before treatment.

chapters.title: Daily life and other medicines
chapters.intro: Make the plan fit your practical needs.

items.title: Eating, drinking and activity
items.text: Aim for tolerable meals and fluids; contact the team if intake falls. Gentle activity and rest can be adjusted to your energy. Ask for dietetic help if needed.

items.title: Medicine and supplement checks
items.text: Check new medicines with oncology pharmacy. Warfarin can require closer INR checks; phenytoin levels may need monitoring. Brivudine is an important prohibited interaction.

items.title: Family, work and fertility
items.text: Ask about infection exposure, work, intimacy, contraception, fertility and any caring responsibilities. Use the medicine-specific duration of precautions given by your team.

items.title: Procedures and travel
items.text: Plan transport and support around appointments. Ask which symptoms or blood-count problems affect travel and when to contact the service.

chapters.title: Review, recovery and follow-up
chapters.intro: Your plan can change as treatment progresses.

items.title: Dose changes are individual
items.text: A pause or reduction may be needed because of symptoms, blood results or kidney function. The team considers the treatment aim and other options.

items.title: After the last dose
items.text: Keep reporting new or persistent symptoms after treatment ends. Your team confirms follow-up, scans and recovery support; the timeline is not a forecast.

items.title: Prepare for review
items.text: Bring questions, symptoms and missed-dose records. Tell the team what matters most to you and ask them to explain the next decision.

questions.q: What is the aim of my treatment?
questions.a: Capecitabine tablets are given with pelvic radiotherapy for locally advanced rectal cancer. The tablets help the radiation treatment work; your team confirms how this fits with surgery and other treatment.

questions.q: Which days do I take the tablets?
questions.a: Capecitabine twice daily on Days 1–5 of each 7-day cycle, alongside radiotherapy, for up to 5–6 cycles. Follow the written plan for treatment days and interruptions.

questions.q: What if I forget a dose or vomit?
questions.a: Do not take an extra dose. Take the next planned dose at its usual time unless treatment has been stopped; report repeated vomiting and check with the team if unsure.

questions.q: When should I stop tablets and call?
questions.a: Stop capecitabine and contact oncology for significant diarrhoea, painful mouth or hand-foot symptoms affecting activity, vomiting that prevents drinking, fever or sudden illness. Do not restart after a toxicity interruption until the team advises.

questions.q: Why do I need blood tests if I take tablets at home?
questions.a: Blood counts, kidney and liver results, together with symptoms, guide whether to continue and at what dose.

questions.q: Do I need a port or a pump?
questions.a: No take-home chemotherapy pump is used. Capecitabine is swallowed, so a central line is not required just to give it.
Ask for your review and follow-up plan. Continue reporting symptoms after the last dose; further therapy depends on the treatment aim and response.

questions.q: Which checks continue when treatment changes or finishes?
questions.a: Keep reviewing bowel, bladder, skin, fatigue and nutrition effects during and after the course. Late effects and surgical assessment follow the radiation/colorectal team plan. Do not automatically extend tablets to make up missed radiation days or continue beyond the planned course.

anatomy: Painful ulcers or reduced intake: stop tablets and call.
New chest pain: stop tablets and seek urgent assessment.
Significant diarrhoea, increased output or dehydration needs prompt advice.
Pain or peeling affecting daily activity: stop tablets and call.
Fever, shivers or sudden illness: contact oncology immediately.
Reduced urine, dizziness or inability to drink needs assessment.
Report painful, broken or weeping skin in the treatment area.
Report urinary pain and discuss fertility and sexual effects.

evidence.title: Why this treatment is offered
evidence.intro: Capecitabine was an effective oral alternative to infused fluorouracil when combined with radiotherapy in the study. Outcomes included the whole treatment programme, including surgery.
evidence.interpretation: Capecitabine was an effective oral alternative to infused fluorouracil when combined with radiotherapy in the study. Outcomes included the whole treatment programme, including surgery.
evidence.population: 1,608 stage II/III rectal cancer patients receiving preoperative chemoradiation, then surgery.
evidence.limitations: Results concern the full multimodality programme; trial schedule changed during recruitment. No isolated tablet-course survival benefit can be inferred.
